review.material: The full public publisher text and 18-page PDF were read, including historical approaches, Complications, Things and Discussion. The cube-subtraction figure was inspected.
review.limitations: Earlier works are discussed through Knight’s review, not independently re-reviewed in this guide. The knotting example is a conceptual demonstration, not a performance trial.

evidence.locator: Introduction and Shapes/Shapes and Other Descriptions, pp. 963–971
evidence.description: Primary historical account of shape-based material descriptions.
Examples expose differences between spatial fusion and physical-object identity.
Making grammar proposal, knotting example and qualified future directions.

sections.title: What it is about
sections.text: Knight traces how shape-grammar research has represented physical things and material properties. The paper then proposes reversing the usual starting point: begin with what materials do and how makers sense them, rather than making every material object behave first like a visual shape.

sections.title: Premise and claim
sections.text: Visual shape operations are useful for creative perception, but may be misleading for physical objects. Knight argues that a computational theory of making should preserve the relevant behaviour of its materials while retaining shape grammar’s open-ended relationship between perception and action.

sections.title: Method of argument
sections.text: A historical review distinguishes set-based objects, parallel descriptions and integrated properties such as colours or weights. Counterexamples reveal problems with using shape operations indiscriminately. The paper then summarizes Knight and Stiny’s making-grammar framework through doing, sensing, stuff and things.

sections.title: Examples that carry the argument
sections.text: Subtracting the line representation of one adjacent cube also removes a shared face-edge structure from the other; conversely, adjoining solids can merge and lose their separate identities. Knotting supplies a contrasting model: strings stay distinct when combined, and sensing rules move hand grasps without necessarily changing the string’s configuration.

sections.title: Proposed conclusion
sections.text: Shapes become one kind of thing that a grammar can make, rather than the mandatory foundation for every material description. Designing with shapes can itself be understood as making: seeing and drawing are specialized sensory and active engagements.

sections.title: Limits and unfinished directions
sections.text: The knotting grammar is deliberately schematic. Watercolour painting is described as a more complex prospective case, not a completed formalization. Choosing an algebra for a material is not the same as predicting all its physical properties or demonstrating a working fabrication system.

sections.title: What this changes for a model
sections.text: Ask whether elements should fuse, stay discrete, deform, or acquire irreversible changes. Identify the doing and sensing actions your rules express. A useful representation depends on the activity being studied; visually identical geometry may correspond to materially different things.

In this framework, materials with activity-relevant properties, including abstract spatial elements.
A rule representing attention or perceptual action that need not physically change the thing.
